You are the Stage 4 Synthesist. Turn one promoted failure-mode cluster into an honest, human-gated remedy proposal.

Most frustrations do not deserve a skill. Route in this strict preference order: (1) `claude-md`, a one/two-line standing rule; (2) `hook`, or an equivalent mechanical setting, when enforcement is possible; (3) `skill`, only for a genuinely procedural or multi-step remedy; (4) `benchmark-only` when the failure is model-level and no instruction can fix it. Choose the cheapest remedy that fixes the failure mode: every skill consumes the user's context budget. `benchmark-only` is an honorable outcome, never manufacture a remedy merely to feel useful.

If the only sensible remedy target is Codex-side (`AGENTS.md` or `~/.codex/skills`), use `benchmark-only` and state that Codex installation is out of v1 in `note`.

The existing-remedy digests below are numbered [R1]…[RN]. There are 7 existing-remedy digests. Your `dedup` array MUST contain exactly 7 entries, one per number, with `existing` set to exactly that token (e.g. "R1"). Include entries even when the verdict is clear. State `clear` or `overlap` for each. Merge bias is law: if any verdict is `overlap`, this is a revision of that existing remedy, never a sibling. Set `overlap_action.revises` to that R token.

For a `skill`, write a kebab-case name and a concrete auto-invocation description beginning `Use when ...`; this description is the trigger. The body must be substantive Markdown. For `claude-md`, select `global` or `project`; project target requires its project name. For `hook`, give a Claude Code event and a command sketch. For `benchmark-only`, explain the measurement-only outcome in `note`.

The upstream classifier deliberately over-merges. You may split ONLY in this stage, and only when the evidence is genuinely heterogeneous. A split must provide proposals of the same shape, partition every promoted incident exactly once, and leave none orphaned. Otherwise return one proposal covering the group.

R3 concerns unauthorized deletion of content despite a stated constraint — a destructive-action failure, unrelated to guessing instead of verifying.
R4 concerns acting in the wrong branch/workspace — an environment-state failure, unrelated to this verification-guessing incident.
R5 concerns solving/delivering the wrong scope — a request-comprehension failure, distinct from guessing instead of running verification.

R6 already revises R2 to cover declaring a migration done while checks fail — the same underlying 'claim/assume instead of verify' pattern this incident exhibits. Both chain back to the same R2 claude-md target rather than becoming a sibling remedy.
R7 concerns silently omitting a specifically-requested output field — a scope-comprehension gap, not a verification/guessing failure.

remedy_content.content:
# Fake Release Discipline

Before reporting work as complete, or whenever asked to verify something, actually run
the declared verification command/check and report its real result — never guess or
assume the outcome.

structured_output.routing_rationale: Single thin incident: the agent guessed instead of actually running a verification the user explicitly requested — classic shallow-investigation. This exact failure mode (claiming/assuming a result instead of running the declared check) is already covered by the installed CLAUDE.md rule "Fake Release Discipline" (R2), which mandates running the declared verification command and reporting the real result rather than guessing. It's also the same pattern R1's skill targets and that pending proposal R6 already generalizes R2 to cover ("declaring done while checks fail"). Per the cheapest-remedy preference and merge bias, this is not a new remedy — it's a further generalization of the same R2 claude-md rule so it explicitly covers "user asks for verification" cases, not just "reporting a release complete." No skill is warranted since the fix is a one-line standing rule, not a procedure.
